newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE-Former peasant helps create Chinese capitalism.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Former peasant helps create Chinese capitalism.

text.p: Once denounced as a capitalist, Lu Guanqiu has become a Chinese business success by by bringing Marxism to the market.

Building on the concept of collective production pioneered in China with the People's Communes of the 1960s, Lu has turned a bicycle repair shop into a thriving enterprise with 6,500 workers that sells automobile parts worldwide.
The 54-year-old son of peasants was persecuted during the chaotic decade of the Cultural Revolution for setting up a bicycle repair stand in his hometown.
Now he is chairman of the board and chief economist of the Wanxiang Group Co, China's biggest maker of universal joints with assets worth five billion yuan ($602.41 million).
It is the parent of 32 companies, including Wanxiang Qian, which was listed as a local currency A share on the Shenzhen stock exchange in 1993 at 3.8 yuan per share, and now trades at about 16 yuan.
Five percent of the parent company's assets are listed, with another 10 percent held by the local government and most of the rest by the township, Lu said. He declined to detail his stake.
Profits in 1996 were 278 million yuan, up 39 percent on 1995, he said. Export earnings were $50.22 million.
When Lu began the company in 1969, start-up capital totalled just 4,000 yuan.
"He is an inspiration and his legacy has been great," said Mo Xiaoping, 35, director of the board of the Wanxiang Group.
Since his rise from the poverty and hunger that plagued China in the late 1950s and early 1960s, Lu had been offered numerous awards by the Beijing government, Mo said.
"But he has no need of prizes and so turns them all down," Mo said, although Lu did accept a bonus of 440,000 yuan in 1980.
STORY OF SUCCESS IS SIMPLE
Lu says his story is a simple one.

In a recent meeting with foreign journalists, he recounted how in 1959 at age 16 he left Xiaoshan, a small town an hour's drive from Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang province on China's east coast, to find work in a steel mill.

Hard times hit soon after. Like many people who had moved to cities to escape the famine that ravaged the countryside and claimed more than 20 million lives between 1959 and 1962, he returned home to help his family.
"I was asked to farm the land, but I didn't know how so I opened a bicycle repair shop," he said, his thick provincial accent making translation to standard Chinese indispensible.
He soon branched out and began making simple farm implements for the local peasantry.
"We saw there was no provision in the national economic plan and that there was a market niche," he said.
But the Cultural Revolution, which began in 1966, halted development of the business and Lu was persecuted for his pursuit of capitalist ideals, he said.

"We couldn't develop our company then. During the Cultural Revolution we couldn't get much done, and the pressure of ideology was the most difficult thing to deal with," he said, referring to the national obsession with politics that pervaded every aspect of Chinese life then.
PEOPLE'S COMMUNE BASIS FOR THRIVING TOWNSHIP ENTERPRISE

Frustrated by the political constraints, Lu saw a way to use them productivly and joined the nationwide move to collectivise industry. In 1969, he and six others set up a people's commune in Xiaoshan.
"Because we couldn't develop our business, we opened a people's commune and that is how we have developed to this day," he said.
As the national hysteria subsided, he set about building Wanxiang into a thriving township enterprise that he said has seen profit every year since.
"After the reform and opening (of 1979), things got even better. Before, all the farmers were able to do was farming, and that was considered reasonable," he said.
"We could see that the standard of the tools the farmers used was poor and we did some market research to see what the peasants really needed and what we could do for them," Lu said.
A change in market strategy in the late 1970s was inspired by the decision of China's government to set production quotas for agricultural machinery, he said.

Having thrived outside the dictates of the centrally planned economy, he did not want to be caught in its net. So the company began making items outside the quota system including universal joints and other vehicle parts.
"We saw that parts for farmers' vehicles were in demand and we knew that as the economy developed, roads and cars were going to develop, too," he said.
The company's products now occupy more than 60 percent of the Chinese market and are exported to 34 countries, including Australia, Britain and the United States.
